Project Title: Characterizing the impact of UFS model error and bias on S2S CONUS forecast skill using a hybrid UFS-machine learning approach
Project Goal: The primary goal of this project is to identify how model bias and forecast error in the simulation of specific dynamical modes of climate variability within the Unified Forecast System (UFS) degrade subseasonal forecasts of temperature and precipitation over the contiguous United States (CONUS).
Research Keywords: Artificial Intelligence (AI) / Machine Learning (ML), Dynamics and Nesting, Forecast Skill Metrics, Model & Forecast Guidance, Teleconnections
Project Description: This project addresses how model bias and forecast error in the simulation of specific dynamical modes of climate variability within the UFS degrade subseasonal forecasts of temperature and precipitation over the contiguous United States (CONUS). Key activities utilize Linear Inverse Modeling (LIM) methods to estimate the impact on global UFS subseasonal forecasts of reducing tropical errors related only to the predictable portion of tropical variability, and execute focused modeling sensitivity experiments to establish an upper bound on potential CONUS forecast skill if specific tropically-based dynamical modes were simulated perfectly. Additionally, the research team determines "analysis LIMs" from reanalysis data and "forecast LIMs" from UFS hindcast datasets to study how tropical errors degrade CONUS forecast skill while examining how extratropical teleconnection errors arise and evolve as the model background state drifts from nature towards its own model climate.
Project Benefits: The project directly assists forecasters with understanding the specific errors and biases inherent to key subseasonal forecasting predictors, leading to more skillful and reliable temperature and precipitation forecasts over the CONUS. By producing a dynamical process-based filter, this work informs model developers on which structural configurations will yield the greatest return on investment regarding overall forecast skill improvements. Furthermore, the project builds close collaboration tracks with the NOAA Climate Prediction Center (CPC) to develop a real-time error correction scheme for operational deployment via the NOAA climate test bed environment.

Project Title: Integrated surface physics for coupled hydrometeorology in the UFS for S2S prediction
Project Goal: The primary goal of this project is to extend a high-resolution, hydrologically-enhanced land-hydrology modeling system to the global domain. This effort aims to improve land surface model sophistication, land surface hydrology representation, and the representation of terrestrial processes interacting with the atmosphere to enhance operational forecast skill and model fidelity across a range of time scales.
Research Keywords: Coupled Models & Techniques, Dynamics and Nesting, Forecast Skill Metrics, Verification & Validation
Associated Forecast Systems & Models: National Water Model (NWM), Noah Multiparameterization Land Surface Model (Noah-MP LSM), Unified Forecast System (UFS), Weather Research and Forecasting Model (WRF), Weather Research and Forecasting Model - Hydro (WRF-Hydro)
Project Description: This project leverages existing connections between the NOAA National Water Model (NoahMP/WRF-Hydro) and the NOAA/NCEP Unified Forecast System (UFS) to implement enhanced land-hydrology physical process representations. Key project tasks include constructing an updated global terrestrial hydrology framework across defined river networks, embedding shallow subsurface lateral routing and surface water inundation schemes directly into the UFS land modeling component, and executing retrospective predictability experiments over multiple climate test years. The combined modeling outputs will be evaluated across seasonal horizons to formulate an optimal long-term implementation strategy for operational Earth system model configurations.
Project Benefits: The project provides the UFS with an advanced global land-hydrology modeling capability, establishing a fully closed terrestrial water budget that captures subsurface lateral transports and dynamic catchment routing. These updates directly reduce persistent operational temperature and flux biases, increasing subseasonal-to-seasonal (S2S) precipitation forecast accuracy. Ultimately, these process enhancements provide structural modeling improvements and predictive guidance to support the numerical weather prediction missions of the NCEP Environmental Modeling Center (EMC).

Project Title: Identifying efficient perturbations for initializing subseasonal-to-seasonal ensemble forecasts with the UFS
Project Goal: The primary goal of this project is to establish a comprehensive initialization strategy for the Unified Forecast System (UFS) coupled atmosphere-ocean numerical forecast model that specifically targets improving probabilistic skill scores at subseasonal-to-seasonal (S2S) forecast lead times of 2-8 weeks.
Research Keywords: Coupled Models & Techniques, Data Assimilation and Ensembles, Dynamics and Nesting, Forecast Skill Metrics
Associated Forecast Systems & Models: Global Ensemble Forecast System (GEFS), Unified Forecast System (UFS)
Project Description: This project establishes an innovative initialization methodology for the Unified Forecast System (UFS) coupled atmosphere-ocean numerical forecast framework to enhance probabilistic skill scores at multi-week subseasonal-to-seasonal (S2S) forecast lead times. Key research activities focus on deploying the dynamic mode decomposition (DMD) algorithm to isolate and extract the oscillating eigenfunctions of the Koopman (KM) and Perron-Frobenius (PF) operators from historical reanalysis data. The research team will test the initialization strategy within a simplified cycled coupled data assimilation (CDA) environment, scale the framework to a low-resolution coupled UFS model setup, and perform a series of retrospective reforecast experiments to systematically evaluate its predictive performance against standard singular vector configurations and conventional operational ensemble perturbations.
Project Benefits: The project validates a next-generation ensemble initialization strategy and prepares prototype software ready for operational scaling, ultimately leading to higher accuracy and accuracy margins for public probabilistic subseasonal forecasts. By directly targeting the oscillating eigenfunctions of climate operators, this work allows for an efficient representation of forecast probability distributions to optimize probabilistic skill scores across weeks 2 to 8. The direct operational recipients and beneficiaries of these software developments are NOAA's Environmental Modeling Center (EMC) and the Climate Prediction Center (CPC).

Project Title: MJO and QBO Contributions to U.S. Precipitation Skill at S2S Leads
Project Goal: This project aims to isolate the predictable atmospheric components of joint MJO and QBO teleconnections over North America, identify the root physical causes of driving biases within the FV3 dynamical core, and combine UFS model outputs with statistical empirical lag matrices to enhance subseasonal precipitation and atmospheric river (AR) forecasting skills.
Research Keywords: Coupled Models & Techniques, Forecast Skill Metrics, Post-processing, Probabilistic Weather Forecasting, Teleconnections
Associated Forecast Systems & Models: Finite-Volume Cubed-Sphere Dynamical Core (FV3), Global Ensemble Forecast System (GEFS), Unified Forecast System (UFS)
Project Description: This project evaluates subseasonal-to-seasonal (S2S) precipitation predictability over North America by exploring how low-frequency tropical and stratospheric modes of variability interact to modulate extreme moisture plumes. To assess systematic model drift and teleconnection errors, the research team performs extensive numerical relaxation and "replay" experiments within the uncoupled FV3 Global Forecast System (FV3GFS), smooth-nudging the tropical troposphere and stratospheric circulation blocks over a multi-decade hindcast period. These experiments are analyzed alongside process-oriented diagnostics from the NOAA MDTF package to diagnose specific convective and moisture-sensitive boundary biases within the UFS and global S2S Database archives. Finally, the project integrates UFS dynamical MJO predictions with statistically derived joint probability matrices to build a calibrated hybrid empirical-dynamical forecasting tool, successfully pushing skillful lead windows for wintertime precipitation and atmospheric river landfall occurrences into weeks 4, 5, and beyond.
Project Benefits: This work advances the fundamental scientific understanding of tropical-extratropical climate drivers, clarifying how stratospheric states modify global wave propagation mechanics to cause severe rainfall, flooding, and storm anomalies. Additionally, the project reinforces the regional meteorology workforce by directly funding and integrating graduate students and postdoctoral researchers into close, collaborative technical pipelines with federal atmospheric scientists

Project Title: Ensemble Prediction and Predictability of Extreme Weather via Circulation Regimes
Project Goal: This project aims to advance the subseasonal to seasonal predictive capacity of high-impact extreme weather events-specifically storminess and precipitation-over the continental United States by leveraging the inherent predictability of planetary-scale circulation regimes to weight multi-model ensemble forecast probabilities
Research Keywords: Coupled Models & Techniques, Data Assimilation and Ensembles, Reanalysis & Reforecasting, Teleconnections
Associated Forecast Systems & Models: Coupled Forecast System (CFSv2), Global Ensemble Forecast System (GEFS), North American Multi-Model Ensemble (NMME), Unified Forecast System (UFS)
Project Description: This project tackles subseasonal-to-seasonal (S2S) prediction challenges by capitalizing on preferred regional atmospheric flow structures (circulation regimes) that display greater predictability than highly parameterized grid-scale fields. Using k-means cluster analysis applied to daily 500 hPa height anomalies from ERA-Interim reanalyses, reference baseline regimes are defined over the Euro-Atlantic and Pacific-North American domains across overlapping multi-month seasons. Multi-model ensemble subseasonal forecasts from SubX and NCEP's Unified Forecast System (UFS), along with seasonal hindcasts from the NMME, are bias-corrected and mapped to these reference centroids using strict pattern correlation metrics. Observed extreme records-encompassing temperature and precipitation anomalies, storm track variances, and atmospheric river occurrences-are composited by regime to map clear, localized conditional hazard frequencies. Finally, the model outputs generate automated daily hazard projections as a linear function of forecasted regime probabilities, validating whether tracking large-scale circulation patterns yields structurally superior skill scores over raw direct model fields beyond typical two-week lead windows.
Project Benefits: This initiative improves the skill and reliability of operational extended-range weather forecasts, providing a methodologically sound alternative that bypasses model sensitivity issues with precipitation parameterizations. The successful transition of the predictive code into NOAA CPC's live environment directly enriches operational hazardous weather outlooks and empirical threat guides. Additionally, the project actively fosters federal workforce development by fully funding a graduate student researcher and facilitating direct technical internships at the Climate Prediction Center, maximizing multi-sector research-to-operations collaboration.

Project Title: S2S Forecasting of North American Precipitation Anomalies: Using Empirical Forecasts to Challenge Dynamical Forecasts
Project Goal: This project aims to evaluate and challenge the subseasonal-to-seasonal predictability of North American precipitation anomalies as simulated by enhanced versions of the Unified Forecast System by using the empirical STRIPES index to isolate Madden-Julian Oscillation teleconnection errors.
Research Keywords: Coupled Models & Techniques, Forecast Skill Metrics, Model & Forecast Guidance, Teleconnections
Project Description: This project addresses systemic predictive shortfalls in subseasonal-to-seasonal forecasts of precipitation by conducting a diagnostic evaluation of multi-model global applications. The research team compares an operational configuration of the Unified Forecast System against two enhanced variations incorporating innovative representation architectures developed under prior NOAA funding. The evaluation isolates three major prediction failure modes: core simulations of the tropical Madden-Julian Oscillation, the spatial and temporal propagation of midlatitude atmospheric teleconnections, and localized precipitation sub-element microphysics. This assessment is mathematically steered by the empirical Subseasonal to Seasonal Teleconnection Response Index for Precipitation as an Evaluation Metric (STRIPES), which tracks the regional strength, consistency, and lag of midlatitude environmental anomalies triggered by remote tropical convective systems. By executing 21 AMIP simulations, the research directly maps systematic spatial and temporal errors to guide NOAA developers in refining physical core structures.
Project Benefits: This work enhances operational subseasonal predictive capabilities by establishing transparent diagnostic benchmarks that identify specific modeling flaws in the simulation of tropical-extratropical interactions. The diagnostic feedback helps NOAA model developers at the Climate Prediction Center and Earth System Research Laboratories target parameterized convection deficiencies within the Unified Forecast System framework. Furthermore, the initiative advances academic-federal integration by directly supporting a graduate student and providing advanced diagnostic software indices to the atmospheric science community.

Project Title: Benefits of stochastic parameterization on the sub-seasonal to seasonal timescales in hindcasts with CESM and UFS
Project Goal: This project will evaluate the performance benefits of unifying and implementing a stochastic parameterization suite within the Unified Forecast System and the Community Earth System Model to improve probabilistic precipitation and surface temperature forecast skill on subseasonal-to-seasonal timescales.
Research Keywords: Coupled Models & Techniques, Data Assimilation and Ensembles, Reanalysis & Reforecasting, Parameterization, Teleconnections
Associated Forecast Systems & Models: Coupled Forecast System (CFSv2), Global Ensemble Forecast System (GEFS), Unified Forecast System (UFS)
Project Description: This project investigates the impact of stochastic parameterization schemes on subseasonal-to-seasonal (S2S) timescales, specifically evaluating forecasts within lead times of 2 to 6 weeks. The research team implements a unified suite of three distinct stochastic schemes-the Stochastic Perturbed Physics-Tendency scheme (SPPT), the Stochastic Kinetic Energy Backscatter Scheme (SKEBS), and the Stochastic Boundary Layer Humidity Perturbations scheme (SHUM)-across both the Unified Forecast System (UFS) and the Community Earth System Model (CESM). The research approach first utilizes multi-decadal uninitialized climate simulations to evaluate structural impacts on systematic model drift, tropical-extratropical teleconnection patterns related to MJO and ENSO, and localized precipitation biases. Following this characterization phase, the project executes extensive 10-member initialized ensemble hindcasts conforming to the SubX protocol across a 17-year historical database to perform rigorous deterministic and probabilistic verification of near-surface temperatures and precipitation fields.
Project Benefits: This research establishes foundational guidance on the utility of stochastic dynamic methods for extended-range prediction systems, specifically reducing systematic climate model errors and improving ensemble spread and reliability. The integration of unified physics suites within CCPP-compliant infrastructures directly assists NCEP Environmental Modeling Center (EMC) and Climate Prediction Center (CPC) developers in configuring future global operational ensemble systems. Additionally, the project enhances multi-institution collaborative links across academic centers, cooperative institutes, and federal research laboratories while providing open open-access hindcast datasets to the wider atmospheric research community.

Project Title: Diagnosing and Improving Unified Forecast System precipitation through observationally constrained stochastic parameterizations
Project Goal: This project will diagnose and improve subseasonal-to-seasonal global precipitation forecasts within the Unified Forecast System and Global Forecast System by replacing ad hoc representations with observationally constrained stochastic parameterizations based on short-range initial forecast error statistics.
Research Keywords: Coupled Models & Techniques, Data Assimilation and Ensembles, Reanalysis & Reforecasting, Parameterization
Associated Forecast Systems & Models: Global Ensemble Forecast System (GEFS), Unified Forecast System (UFS)
Project Description: his project addresses global model prediction errors on subseasonal-to-seasonal timescales by replacing ad hoc stochastic suites with observationally constrained formulations of the Stochastic Perturbed Physics-Tendency scheme. The research framework leverages the initial tendency and short-range forecast error statistics from the atmospheric core of the Unified Forecast System to systematically calculate time-varying budget residuals with respect to operational data assimilation analyses. By moving beyond ad hoc space-time covariance assumptions, the project uses the derived error diagnostics and multi-decadal Linear Inverse Models to dynamically constrain specified random perturbations over key multi-scale interface regions such as the Indo-Pacific Warm Pool and Maritime Continent. The optimized configurations are tested through extensive 80-member ensemble reanalyses and 30-member reforecasts across a multi-year baseline period to isolate deterministic and probabilistic improvements in precipitation skill curves and higher-order statistical vertical velocity moments.
Project Benefits: This initiative enhances the scientific accuracy and predictive reliability of operational extended-range precipitation and data assimilation frameworks, directly benefiting centers that rely on the Unified Forecast System for ancillary products. The resulting observationally constrained parameterization codes are documented and shared via open-source repositories to provide the wider meteorological community with a structured methodology for stochastifying coupled Earth system components. Furthermore, the multi-agency project structure reinforces key technical links between cooperative institutes, national climate prediction groups, and operational model developers at the Environmental Modeling Center.

Project Title: Assessment and calibration of extreme precipitation probabilities in S2S forecast models
Project Goal: This project aims to identify, assess, and calibrate state-dependent systematic biases in extreme liquid and frozen precipitation within submonthly multi-model ensemble forecasts using process-based regression techniques conditioned on large-scale atmospheric variables.
Research Keywords: Forecast Skill Metrics, Model & Forecast Guidance, Post-processing, Probabilistic Weather Forecasting
Associated Forecast Systems & Models: Global Ensemble Forecast System (GEFS), Unified Forecast System (UFS)
Project Description: This project will investigate the state-dependence of systematic extreme rainfall and snowfall biases in submonthly forecasts ranging from week-2 to week-4 leads across the SubX and WMO S2S multi-model database suites. Unlike conventional unconditional post-processing calibrations that apply uniform offsets based strictly on lead window and target period, this research develops state-dependent, process-based calibration methods. The developed models use quantile regression and conditional distributions to map how simulated rainfall extremes scale with background environmental factors including near-surface temperature, dew-point temperature, and convective available potential energy. These physical relations are integrated as covariates into extended logistic regression formulations, producing calibrated probabilistic projections. The performance of these process-based corrections is benchmarked against existing operational schemes through head-to-head statistical skill matrices, with an added expansion to evaluate week-2 frozen precipitation predictability for operational hazardous snowfall guidance.
Project Benefits: This initiative improves the skill and structural utility of extended-range probabilistic hazard outlooks, equipping forecasters with objective guidance criteria to map precipitation extremes with higher regional precision. The resulting process-based calibration scripts are open-sourced via GitHub to provide the modeling enterprise with a transparent tool for state-dependent error diagnostics. Additionally, the close collaborative architecture directly links university researchers with federal applied scientists at the Climate Prediction Center, immediately transferring diagnostic software code to refine operational model datasets and support safe community decision-making.
